system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2180-01-21 11:33:00 to 2180-01-22 15:13:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of liver transplant presented for elective repair of a symptomatic right inguinal hernia. He underwent an open Bassini repair without complications. Postoperatively, he experienced moderate pain requiring tramadol, which led to an overnight stay for pain management. By the next morning, his pain was well controlled, he was ambulating independently, and his incision was clean and dry. He was discharged home with instructions on wound care, activity restrictions, and medication changes, including a switch from sirolimus to tacrolimus and the addition of ferrous sulfate for anemia. Follow-up was arranged with the transplant and surgical teams.
problems: Inguinal hernia, without mention of obstruction or gangrene, unilateral or unspecified (not specified as recurrent)
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of prostate

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you've been having fevers and chills at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. Last night I spiked a fever up to 101.3. I was shaking so hard I couldn’t stop. Just felt awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any cough, sore throat, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. No chest pain either. Just tired and shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any belly pain, nausea, or changes in urination?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, stomach feels fine. Bowels are normal. No burning when I pee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history—liver transplant, diabetes, recent hernia surgery—we want to be careful. We’ve sent blood and urine tests to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on a lot of meds since the transplant. Rapamune, tacrolimus, Myfortic…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and those help prevent rejection, but they also make you more vulnerable to infections. We’re also checking your kidney function and electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys have been a little off lately. Creatinine was around 2.3 before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Today it’s 3.0, so a bit higher. Could be from dehydration during the fever. We’re giving you fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, and my potassium came back high in the ER, didn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 6.2, which is concerning. But your EKG was normal, and we gave you kayexalate and insulin to bring it down. It’s already improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be from my meds? I know tacrolimus can affect kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Both tacrolimus and the Bactrim you take for prevention can contribute. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back clear—no pneumonia. Stool test was negative for C. diff. No signs of infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the fever then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be a virus. We’re not starting antibiotics unless we find something. Your exam is otherwise normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a fever like this a few weeks ago. They thought it was viral then too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. We’ll keep monitoring your temperature and repeat labs tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More tired than feverish now. Still a bit shaky, but no chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re afebrile now, which is a positive sign. We’ll keep you hydrated and monitor your kidney numbers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Evening check-in. Your potassium is down to 5.3 and creatinine improved to 2.5. That’s trending in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Should I stop any of my usual meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your Lasix for now—don’t want to worsen the kidney issue. Otherwise, continue everything except we’re adjusting your transplant meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs this morning look better. Potassium is 4.2—normal. Creatinine is 2.4, still coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile all night. Blood cultures are still pending, but so far no growth. Likely viral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my transplant meds? I was on both tacrolimus and sirolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sirolimus level came back at 6.7, which is therapeutic. So we’re stopping tacrolimus and increasing sirolimus to 4 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why stop tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it can affect kidneys and potassium. Since your sirolimus is now at a good level, we can rely on that instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding it for now. Restart it after your liver clinic visit. They’ll guide that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re feeling better, labs are improving, and no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take sirolimus 4 mg daily—stop the tacrolimus. Continue Myfortic, Bactrim, and your other meds as listed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Get your sirolimus level checked next week and see the transplant clinic. Call to confirm the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay without tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Sirolimus is now at a good level, and this change helps protect your kidneys. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Nurse will go over your meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Stop tacrolimus, increase sirolimus, hold Lasix, follow up next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re alert, walking fine, and feeling well. We’re discharging you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and call if you develop fever, swelling, or feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of liver transplant, diabetes, and recent hernia repair was admitted for evaluation of fevers and chills at home. He was found to have hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, likely prerenal in origin due to reduced intake during illness. He was treated with kayexalate and IV fluids, with improvement in potassium and renal function. Infectious workup was negative, including normal chest X-ray, negative C. diff toxin, and no growth in urine culture; blood cultures later identified Enterobacter cloacae complex but were interpreted in the context of likely contamination. The fever resolved without antibiotics, presumed viral. Tacrolimus was discontinued and sirolimus increased to 4 mg daily given therapeutic levels and concern for tacrolimus-related nephrotoxicity. Lasix was held during admission. The patient was discharged home afebrile with follow-up arranged in the transplant clinic and instructions to monitor sirolimus levels.
